S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
examples: Focuses at first during class or meetings but soon becomes distracted or spaces out.
Re-reads the same paragraph in a book multiple times but the content does not register.
Loses focus while watching movies or TV and misses the plot.
Unable to maintain attention until the end of a long meeting or lecture, often drifting off or becoming drowsy.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
examples: Starts homework or projects but fails to complete them, submitting unfinished work or missing deadlines.
When given multi-step instructions, follows only the first few steps and forgets the rest.
Starts cleaning or organizing but switches to another task midway, failing to finish.
Leaves almost completed work reports or paperwork unfinished, neglecting the final steps.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
examples: Desk, bag, or room is always messy and remains disorganized.
Unable to prioritize or determine the order of tasks, starting them randomly.
Fails to plan time effectively, frequently missing deadlines or rushing to finish at the last minute.
Feels overwhelmed by how to start multi-step projects and procrastinates.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
examples: Constantly shaking legs or twisting and squirming body while seated.
Spinning a pen or fiddling with nearby objects, unable to keep hands still.
Continually changing posture and feeling uncomfortable while sitting.
Constantly moving, such as tapping the desk with fingers or tapping feet on the floor.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
examples: Frequently leaves seat or wanders around during class or meetings using excuses.
Unable to sit still during meals and keeps getting up.
Leaves seat in the middle of a movie or performance to go to the restroom or go outside.
Continually leaves seat and wanders around in the office where one is expected to sit and work.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
examples: Feels uncomfortable and restless as if something is squirming inside when sitting still.
Feels internally anxious and stifled in situations requiring prolonged sitting.
A sense of urgency and anxiety that one must keep moving or doing something.
Feels unable to endure staying still and must constantly be doing something.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
examples: Raises hand or blurts out the answer before the question is even finished in class or meetings.
Jumps to conclusions and speaks before the other person finishes their sentence.
Answers hastily without reading the question to the end in quizzes or exams.
Interrupts and answers in the middle of a conversation without listening to the other person until the end.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
examples: Cannot wait and cuts in line or gets impatient when standing in a queue.
Rushes or cuts in without waiting for their turn in games or board games.
Keeps checking the time or complaining when waiting for their turn at hospitals or public offices.
Fidgets, complains, or gets annoyed in situations where waiting for a turn is required.

symptom.disease_info: Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Hyperactive/Impulsive Presentation) is characterized mainly by developmentally inappropriate levels of motor activity, restlessness, impulsive decision-making, and difficulty inhibiting responses, with inattention often present but less prominent. It typically begins in childhood and persists into adolescence and adulthood, with functional impairment in academic, occupational, or social domains required for diagnosis. Clinically, patients may come to attention when environmental demands for sustained effort, planning, or behavioral restraint increase, such as during higher education or more complex jobs. It is distinguished from mood, anxiety, or disruptive behavior disorders by its early onset, cross-situational pervasiveness, and the pattern of chronic hyperactive/impulsive traits rather than episodic changes in behavior.

patient.stressor: Cathy had long relied on her intelligence and love of fast-paced problem-solving to succeed in software development, and her tendency to pace, gesture, and multitask during coding sessions was tolerated in startup environments. About two years ago, after being promoted to a senior role leading agile teams in a larger company, her days shifted from mostly hands-on coding to long planning meetings, code reviews, and mentoring sessions that demanded patient, sustained engagement and careful listening. In this more structured context, her long-standing restlessness and urge to move became harder to hide: colleagues noticed her frequently leaving her chair during sprints, drifting over to other desks mid-meeting, and appearing disengaged in video calls, which began to be reflected in performance feedback about her leadership presence. When a trusted manager framed the issue as a possible attention-regulation problem rather than a motivation issue and suggested an evaluation—echoing Cathy’s own worries about how hard it felt to simply stay put in meetings—she sought psychiatric consultation to understand and address what was interfering with her effectiveness at work.
patient.chief_complaint: “In longer work meetings I just can’t stay in my seat—I keep getting up to move around even when I know it looks unprofessional.”

S002.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
S002.description: Often has difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.
S002.manifestation: On longer Zoom calls, I notice that after the first ten minutes my mind drifts off to random ideas about other projects or what I’m making for dinner, and then I suddenly realize I’ve missed a chunk of what my team just agreed on.

S004.name: Instruction_Follow through_Difficulty
S004.description: Often does not follow through on instructions and fails to finish schoolwork, chores, or duties in the workplace.
S004.manifestation: My manager will ask me to, say, review a pull request, write feedback, and then update the Jira ticket, and I’ll do the first part enthusiastically but then get sidetracked by a new email and forget to actually finish the last steps unless someone reminds me.

S005.name: Organization_Difficulty
S005.description: Often has difficulty organizing tasks and activities.
S005.manifestation: When I sit down on Monday to plan my week, all the different tickets, meetings, and mentoring tasks just blur together, and I end up bouncing between them instead of following a clear order, so things only get done when they become urgent.

S010.name: Fidgeting
S010.description: Often fidgets with or taps hands or feet or squirms in seat.
S010.manifestation: In meetings I’m constantly bouncing my leg, clicking my pen, or twisting my hair without even realizing it, and I only notice when someone glances at me or I see myself fidgeting in the little video window.

S011.name: Leaving_Seat
S011.description: Often leaves seat in situations when remaining seated is expected.
S011.manifestation: In these longer planning sessions, I’ll find myself standing up to refill my water, straighten the whiteboard, or check something on another screen every 15 or 20 minutes, even when I know I don’t actually need to move and it probably looks like I’m not engaged.

S012.name: Feeling_Restless
S012.description: Often runs about or climbs in situations where it is inappropriate. (Note: In adolescents or adults, may be limited to feeling restless.)
S012.manifestation: Any time I have to sit still for more than half an hour—like during all-hands meetings or my kids’ school assemblies—I get this pent-up, jittery feeling in my body, like I need to stretch or walk around or I’m going to crawl out of my skin.

S016.name: Blurting_Answers
S016.description: Often blurts out an answer before a question has been completed.
S016.manifestation: In one-on-ones, I have a habit of jumping in with solutions or finishing my engineers’ sentences before they’ve fully explained the problem, because my brain races ahead and I feel this urge to say it right away.

S017.name: Waiting_Turn_Difficulty
S017.description: Often has difficulty waiting his or her turn.
S017.manifestation: Whether it’s waiting my turn to speak in a big group meeting or standing in line at the coffee shop, I get noticeably impatient and antsy, checking my phone or shifting around and feeling annoyed that everything is moving so slowly.

add_requirements.onset_prior_to_age_12_years: Even back in elementary school, teachers were always telling my parents that I couldn’t stay in my seat, that I blurted out answers, and that I was constantly walking around the classroom when I was supposed to be working quietly.
add_requirements.functional_impairment: Over the past couple of years, my performance reviews have started to mention that I seem distracted and not fully present in meetings, and I’ve been passed over to lead a couple of high-visibility projects because my managers worry about how I come across in longer planning sessions.
add_requirements.duration: These issues have really started to interfere with my work since I moved into this senior role about two years ago, when my days shifted to longer, more structured meetings instead of mostly hands-on coding.
